sections.h: The book of Nahum in one page
sections.b: Nahum of Elkosh is the only prophet whose whole book is one oracle against a foreign city. It has three chapters: a hymn to the LORD as avenger and refuge (1:2-8), a turn between Nineveh and Judah with the herald of 1:15, a poem of the attack (chapter 2), and a funeral song with woes (chapter 3). It is dated between the fall of Thebes (about 663 BC) and the fall of Nineveh (612 BC).

common: The book was written in the 600s BC, before or close to the fall of Nineveh in 612 BC.
uncommon: Alfred Haldar (1947) read it as a liturgy of a cult prophet; a few read chapters 2-3 as written after the fall.

sections.b: Nahum is the second book of the Twelve about Nineveh. Jonah, set a century or more earlier, tells how the city repented and was spared; Nahum, in the 600s BC, announces its fall, which came in 612 BC when the Babylonians and Medes took it. Nahum calls it the city of bloodshed (3:1) and a prostitute who sells nations (3:4). It does not mention Jonah's Nineveh at all.

common: Nahum's Nineveh is the Assyrian capital shortly before its destruction.

sections.h: The end of Assyria in Nahum
sections.b: Nahum reads Assyria's power as a yoke on Judah (1:13) and promises its end (1:15; 3:18-19). The Babylonian Chronicle gives the facts: Nineveh fell in 612 BC and the last Assyrian army held out at Harran until about 609. Nahum does not name a king. Isaiah 10 and 37 and Zephaniah 2:13-15 tell the same story from other points in the century.

common: The prophets present Assyria as the LORD's rod that is then judged for its pride.

sections.h: A jealous God who takes vengeance (Nahum 1:2-8)
sections.b: Nahum 1:2-8 opens with three lines of vengeance (naqam) and a God who is jealous, slow to anger, and will not leave guilt unpunished. The mercy clauses of the Exodus creed (Exodus 34:6-7) are left out, and the hymn turns on 1:7: the LORD is good and a stronghold to those who shelter in him. Readers have asked whether the vengeance is a judge's act or a god's mood, and the Plain English Translation's answer, with Deuteronomy 32:35 and Psalm 94:1, is that it is the first.

common: God's vengeance in the Bible is the act of a judge setting wrong right.
uncommon: Isaac the Syrian taught that wrath is the way God's love is felt by those who resist it (the treatise is not identified here).

sections.b: Hermann Gunkel (1893) noticed that the lines of Nahum 1:2-8 open with the first letters of the Hebrew alphabet, from aleph on, but the pattern breaks off and has gaps. Christensen (1975) reworked it by rearranging the text. Many recent commentators call it at most partial. The Plain English Translation does not rewrite the Hebrew to fit it.

common: The hymn has an incomplete alphabetic pattern.
uncommon: The full pattern can be restored if the text is rearranged (Christensen).

sections.h: Nahum and the siege of Nineveh
sections.b: Nahum is a war oracle: the LORD declares "Look, I am against you" (2:13; 3:5), the LORD of Armies sends the destroyer, and the city falls. Unlike the conquest of Canaan, no Israelite army takes part. Judah is told to keep its festivals (1:15). The war is the LORD's alone and is carried out by a foreign power.

common: Nahum's war is fought by foreign armies, not by Israel.

sections.h: The storm and the sea in Nahum 1
sections.b: Nahum 1:3-6 has the full pattern of the divine warrior: the LORD comes in gale and storm, rebukes the sea and rivers, withers Bashan, Carmel and Lebanon, makes the mountains shake and the rocks break. Nothing in the poem says he marches from the south; the focus is on nature's defeat. Compare Habakkuk 3 and Psalm 18.

common: The hymn uses storm imagery shared with Canaanite and Mesopotamian poetry.

sections.b: The question "Who can stand when he is indignant?" asks what Malachi 3:2 and Revelation 6:17 ask of the day of the LORD. Nahum does not use the phrase "day of the LORD"; the coming of the LORD in storm and flood is the same kind of event, seen as the end of one empire.

common: The coming of the LORD in judgment is described in the same terms across the prophets.

sections.h: Nahum, a prophet of one city
sections.b: Nahum is unusual among the prophets: his book is addressed to a foreign city, names no king of Judah, and says almost nothing about Judah's sin. Critics ask whether it is a prophecy of salvation of the kind Jeremiah warns about (Jeremiah 28:8-9) and answer that it speaks for Judah's oppressed, not against Judah's own truthfulness. Jonah and Nahum together show the prophets speaking to a foreign power on opposite occasions.

common: Nahum is a prophet of consolation to Judah and judgment on Assyria.

sections.h: Nahum, the second word on Nineveh
sections.b: Jonah ends with God's question about pity for Nineveh (4:11). Nahum, in a book set a century or more after Jonah's, ends with a question about Nineveh's wickedness (3:19). Both quote the creed of Exodus 34:6-7, Jonah for its mercy (4:2) and Nahum for its warning (1:3). In both orders of the Twelve Jonah comes before Nahum. Tobit 14 (in the deuterocanonical Tobit) names Nahum as the prophet of Nineveh's fall in Codex Sinaiticus, the text the site's Tobit follows, and Jonah in Codex Vaticanus.
sections.refs: Nahum 1:3; Nahum 3:19; Jonah 1:2; Jonah 4:2; Jonah 4:11; Tobit 14:4

common: Nahum is read as the sequel to Jonah: the city's repentance did not last.

sections.b: In the Hebrew order Nahum follows Micah and comes before Habakkuk (Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum...); in the Greek order Jonah comes immediately before Nahum. The catchwords between Jonah and Nahum are the creed (Jonah 4:2; Nahum 1:3), Nineveh and the word for "wickedness" (Jonah 1:2; Nahum 3:19). Editors (Nogalski, Sweeney) treat Nahum as the answer to Jonah's mercy.

common: The Twelve are one scroll in Jewish tradition.
uncommon: The Twelve was edited as one book with links between neighbors (Nogalski, Schart); others doubt it (Ben Zvi).

sections.b: Nahum 3:4 calls Nineveh a charming prostitute and a mistress of sorceries who "sells nations." Here zenunim, "acts of prostitution," is a figure of seduction, trade and treaties, not of a people's faithlessness to the LORD as in Hosea. Isaiah 23:15-17 does the same for Tyre, and Revelation 17-18 for Babylon.

common: The image of a city as a prostitute is a prophetic figure for political and commercial seduction.

sections.b: Nahum names keshafim, "sorceries," among Nineveh's sins. Assyrian kings relied on omens and exorcists (the library of Ashurbanipal), and the prophets list the same offense for Jezebel (2 Kings 9:22) and Babylon (Isaiah 47:9, 12).

Nahum 3:5-7 has the LORD lift the city's skirts over her face, show nations her nakedness and pelt her with filth. The same image is in Hosea 2:10, Jeremiah 13:26, Ezekiel 16:37 and Isaiah 47:3. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew. Critics (Weems, Yee, O'Brien) say the image takes violence against women as a picture of God's justice, with God as the speaker; others say it is the standard picture of a conquered city and that the shaming falls on the aggressor. Ortlund (1996) defends the marriage metaphor within a theology of God's unfaithful wife, and Keefe (2001) reads the woman's body as a figure for the social body of the nation; both write on Hosea and the prophets in general, not on Nahum. 3:10 also describes the smashing of Thebes' children.
sections.refs: Nahum 3:5; Nahum 3:6; Nahum 3:10; Hosea 2:10; Jeremiah 13:26; Ezekiel 16:37; Isaiah 47:3

common: The text uses a female figure for the city; its violence is real and debated.
uncommon: Some read it as a mirror: Nineveh suffers what it did to others.

sections.b: Nahum 3:15-17 uses the locust three ways: the fire and sword eat Nineveh as locusts eat a field; Nineveh is told to "multiply like the locust"; and her officials are like locusts on a cold wall that vanish in the sun. The words are yeleq ("the hopping locust," as in Joel 1:4), 'arbeh ("locust") and a swarm (Amos 7:1).

Nahum names Cush first among Thebes' strengths. The Cushite pharaohs of the 25th Dynasty ruled Egypt until the Assyrians drove them south; Taharqa (Tirhakah) is the Cushite king of 2 Kings 19:9. The Cushite defeat at Thebes in about 663 BC is the background to the verse.

Nahum 3:8-10 holds up Egypt's old capital to Nineveh. Thebes, behind the Nile and its canals, with Cush, Egypt, Put and Libya as allies, still went into exile when Assyria took it about 663 BC. Jeremiah 46:25 and Ezekiel 30:14-16 later name the same city in their oracles on Egypt.

sections.h: Nahum, an oracle against one city
sections.b: Nahum is a whole book of an oracle against a nation (a massa'). Unlike Amos 1-2 or Isaiah 13-23, it has no sins of Israel to set beside the nation's, and unlike Jonah it contains no repentance. Its form combines a victory song, a funeral song and woes.

sections.h: Nahum 1:3 and 3:7: the creed and the comfort
sections.b: In Joel 2:13 and Jonah 4:2 the LORD "changes his mind about the harm." Nahum cites the same creed without that clause (1:3) and ends with no comforters for Nineveh (3:7), a word from the same root as nacham, "change one's mind." Readers have taken this to show that God's change of mind depends on the people's turning (Jeremiah 18:7-10), that Nineveh's turning did not last, or that the creed can be used both ways.
sections.refs: Nahum 1:3; Nahum 3:7; Joel 2:13; Jonah 3:10; Jonah 4:2; Jeremiah 18:7

common: The Exodus creed has a merciful half and a punishing half; the Twelve quotes each in different books.

sections.b: Nahum 1:14 says the LORD will cut off the carved image and the cast image from the house of Nineveh's gods, and 3:6 has him throw "detestable things" (shiqqutsim, the idol word) at the city. Sennacherib was murdered in the house of his god (2 Kings 19:37).

The questions of 2:11 ("Where is the lions' lair now?"), the woe-cry of 3:1 (hoy, the cry at a funeral) and the closing images of 3:18-19 are the language of lament turned on an enemy. Compare Lamentations 4:21 for Edom and Isaiah 14:4-21 for Babylon.

Nahum 2:2 promises that the LORD will bring back the pride of Jacob "like the pride of Israel": either Judah and the northern kingdom, or one people twice named. It is a short promise of restoration set inside a war poem.

Nahum 3:18 closes on the shepherds of Assyria asleep and the flock scattered on the mountains. Shepherd was a title of kings. Compare Ezekiel 34:5-6 and Jeremiah 23:1-4, where Israel's flock is scattered when its shepherds fail.

Nahum 3:11 tells Nineveh "You too will be drunk," using the picture of the cup of the LORD's anger (Jeremiah 25:15-29; Isaiah 51:17-23; Habakkuk 2:15-16; Lamentations 4:21). The "too" ties Nineveh to Thebes, who drank before.
After Thebes fell, the captors "cast lots for her honored men." Joel 3:3 and Obadiah 11 use the same phrase for Jerusalem. The lot divided prisoners among the victors.

Nahum 1:15 tells Judah to keep its festivals (chaggim) and pay its vows because the Assyrian is cut off. The pilgrim feasts of Deuteronomy 16 needed safe roads to Jerusalem. Josiah's Passover (2 Kings 23:21-23) is a possible occasion.

The Medes, with the Babylonians, are the likely attackers behind Nahum 2. The Babylonian Chronicle says they took Ashur in 614 BC and joined the Babylonians to besiege Nineveh in 612. Nahum does not name them.

sections.h: Babylon and the fall of Nineveh
sections.b: Nabopolassar of Babylon, from 626 BC, led the revolt against Assyria that ended with the fall of Nineveh in 612. Nahum does not name Babylon; Zephaniah and Habakkuk point to the Chaldean power the Babylonian Chronicle records.

Nahum 1:15 is the first appearance of the herald whose feet are on the mountains. The Hebrew words are the same as Isaiah 52:7. The runner of 2 Samuel 18 is the human model. Romans 10:15 adapts Isaiah's Greek (not Nahum's) for the preaching of the gospel. The Plain English Translation's "the one who brings good news" renders the Hebrew verb basar, which the Greek Bible translates with euangelizomai.

common: The herald is both a human runner and the pattern for later preachers of good news.

sections.h: The fall of Nineveh in the Babylonian Chronicle
sections.b: The Fall of Nineveh Chronicle (ABC 3) records the years 616 to 609 BC. The Medes took Ashur in 614. In 612 Babylonians and Medes besieged Nineveh for about three months and took it, and the last Assyrian king died. The army at Harran held out until about 609. Josiah of Judah died at Megiddo in 609 after going out to meet Pharaoh Neco, who was marching toward the king of Assyria (2 Kings 23:29; compare 2 Chronicles 35:20-24).

Nahum 3:1 names Nineveh the city of bloodshed ('ir damim), a title Ezekiel gives to Jerusalem (Ezekiel 22:2; 24:6, 9). The book's charge against Nineveh is that its blood-guilt has no end, and the last verse repeats it (3:19).

The Nahum Pesher is the only pesher that names historical figures: "Demetrius king of Greece," Antiochus, and the Lion of Wrath, usually taken as Alexander Jannaeus, who hanged men alive. It reads "the city of bloodshed" as the city of Ephraim, whose people "seek smooth things" (usually taken as the Pharisees). It is the Qumran community's reading, written about 400 years after Nahum's day.

Nahum describes a city's destruction as the LORD's doing, and Christians have asked what that says about human violence. Churches answer differently: some stress that vengeance is God's (Romans 12:19, quoting Deuteronomy 32:35), others allow the sword to rulers in their office, and the Catholic Church allows lawful defense under strict conditions; Anabaptist confessions forbid revenge.

Nahum answers the question of whether the empire's cruelty will be answered. Its comfort is for Judah, whose "yoke" is to be broken (1:13), and its warning is for Nineveh, whose wickedness has "passed over" everyone (3:19). The justice it describes is large-scale, political and final.

Nahum 1:4 has the LORD scold the sea so that it dries, and drain every river, as at the Exodus (Exodus 14:21) and the Jordan (Joshua 3:16). In Canaanite stories the sea is a rival god; Israel's poetry has it both obeying (Psalm 89:9) and broken as an enemy (Psalm 74:13).

sections.h: Josiah and the weakening of Assyria
sections.b: If Nahum belongs to the years when Assyria was weakening, Josiah's reform (2 Kings 22-23) and his death at Megiddo in 609 BC, when he went out to meet Neco as Neco marched toward the king of Assyria (2 Kings 23:29; compare 2 Chronicles 35:20-24), are the Judean background; why Josiah went out is not stated in Kings. Nahum himself names no king of Judah.

The yoke of Nahum 1:13 was heavy on Judah from Ahaz (2 Kings 16:7) through Hezekiah's tribute after 701 BC (2 Kings 18:14-16). Sennacherib's own account boasts that he shut up Hezekiah in Jerusalem "like a bird in a cage."
